item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
As a puzzle-box-minded reader, it is always gratifying when your impressions are confirmed by WoG (or, in a canonless setting, the original author). Although I'm certain I've read a lot of material informed by this tale, this is the first time I've seen the nature of Gears' "emotional neutrality" solidly confirmed.
When unrealistic things happen in fiction, I always look (and usually find) excuses or explanations, and in SCP, the anomalous is the last thing I tend to look toward.
Nobody should last in the Foundation without mental illness. Knowing what they know, while living under the perpetual AND intermittent threats posed by SCPs, would be an intolerable stress on any human mind. Those that cannot be bent, break. Those who are bent, well …
I hope I find more tales, new or old, about the plethora of ways the psyche can defensively distort! Thanks!

…and even though I think it's fairly obvious why Gears ended up as he did, I think it is interesting that in-setting, it's the last thing most characters think of. Not only are they all hyper-vigilant for anomolous explanations, but nobody wants to realize that the best-case and most adaptive scenario for a career researcher might be extreme PTSD resulting in near-total emotional inexpressivity!

item.content:encoded:
I upvoted at:

The officer on the security cameras for that area took almost no notice, logging only “Doctors passed, injured.”

Aside from being a very well-executed character study of Gears this piece also documents the insanity that being in the business of containing and studying SCPs brings with it without resorting to LOLFoundation reports of whacky antics and suicide watches. This one line tells me so much more about the general apathy creep, the emotionally blunting effect of being exposed to a truth that does not belong in a rational worldview.

Bravo.

item.content:encoded:
This is, in my not-so-frakking-humble opinion, a really good story. The tone fits in with Dr. Gears' deliberately detached personality, and helps explain how it became so.

I ran across a quote from an RPG the other day that reminded me of this. The character is from a fantasy RPG (either D&D or GURPS Dungeon Fantasy, apparently); he's a semi-disillusioned old paladin, who's had to compromise his ideals a few times in the interests of the greater good. One piece of advice offered in-character to a new party member:

"To protect everyone's smiles you need to sacrifice your own. Because in the end none of this really is about what YOU want."

I get the feeling from this story that Gears (the character, just to be plain, not the real person) feels the same way about what the Foundation has to do.
